1: Outliers: what they are, why they happen, how to find them, and how to fix them. Lectures nineteen and twenty and practical nineteen and twenty, with Doctor Shital Bhatt.
2: Here is the session map. The lecture covers nine topics: what an outlier is, why outliers occur, four types of outliers, finding them with a box plot, Z score and I Q R, finding them with machine learning models, why outliers spoil results, how to fix outliers, what happens if we do nothing, and repeating it on a second dataset. The practical follows eight steps: load the New York Airbnb data, find why outliers exist, find them with Z score and I Q R, find them with machine learning models, fix them by removing, capping, replacing or taking logs, replace values using machine learning, compare numbers before and after, and compare model accuracy before and after.
3: What is an outlier? An outlier is a value that is very far from the other values in the same column. It is unusual, but not always a mistake. For example, seven staff earn thirty to forty five thousand a month, and the director earns five hundred thousand. The average, the mean, is ninety five thousand, but the middle value, the median, is thirty nine thousand. One person pushed the mean up two and a half times, while the median hardly changed. In short, mean and standard deviation are easily pulled by outliers. Median and I Q R are not.
4: Real data: mean versus median, in the forty eight thousand eight hundred ninety five New York Airbnb homes. Price has a mean of one fifty two point seven two dollars, but a median of one hundred six, and a maximum of ten thousand. Minimum nights has a mean of seven but a median of three, and a maximum of twelve fifty. Number of reviews has a mean of twenty three and a median of five. Reviews per month, host listings count and availability all show the same pattern. The highest price is ten thousand dollars per night, while a typical home costs only one hundred six. In most columns, the mean is much bigger than the median, because a few very large values pull the mean up.
5: Why do outliers occur? Four causes. One, a data entry error: someone typed it wrong, like eleven homes with price zero, and fourteen homes asking for more than three hundred sixty five nights. Two, a genuine extreme: real but very rare, like two hundred thirty nine luxury homes above one thousand dollars a night. Three, a measurement cap: the value was stopped at a maximum limit, like nine hundred sixty five California districts stored at exactly five hundred thousand and one. Four, a different population: the row comes from a different kind of group, like one host who owns three hundred twenty seven homes, which is a company and not a person. First ask why. Mistakes get fixed or removed, real values are kept or capped, and limits are marked.
6: Four types of outliers. Global: very far from all other values, like three Airbnb homes at ten thousand dollars a night, or a two and a half metre tall student. Contextual: normal overall but odd for its group, like two fifty dollars for a shared room, which would be fine for a full home, or thirty degrees Celsius, normal in May but odd in a Delhi December. Collective: each value is normal but the group is odd, like one host listing forty eight rooms at exactly two thirty nine dollars, or twenty small card payments in two minutes. Multivariate: each column is normal but the pair is odd, like eleven point eight reviews a month with only fifteen reviews in total, or height of one fifty centimetres with weight of one ten kilograms.
7: Contextual outliers: check each group separately. The upper fence for entire homes is three ninety two fifty dollars, for private rooms one sixty two fifty, and for shared rooms one thirty eight, while the whole column has a fence of three thirty four. One thousand twenty one homes are too costly for their room type, but look normal when all rooms are mixed together. In short, one limit for everyone misses them, and a separate limit for each room type finds them.
8: How do we find outliers? Three approaches. One, look at a chart: a box plot with dots outside the whiskers, a histogram with a long tail and lonely bars, or a scatter plot with points far from the crowd. Always do this first. Two, use a simple rule: the Z score, flagging absolute z above three, or the I Q R rule, outside Q one minus one point five I Q R to Q three plus one point five I Q R, or the modified Z, flagging above three point five. These check one column at a time. Three, use a machine learning model: Isolation Forest, Local Outlier Factor, or D B SCAN. These check many columns together. Start with a chart, then a simple rule, then a model if you need it.
9: Find outliers by eye with the box plot. The box holds the middle fifty percent of values, the red line is the middle value, the median, the whiskers show the normal range, and the orange dots are outliers outside the normal range. In this data, five of six columns have many dots above the box. Only availability has none.
10: The Z score rule. Z equals x minus the mean, divided by the standard deviation. It tells how many standard deviations a value is from the mean. If z is more than three, or less than minus three, call it an outlier. Use it when data looks like a bell curve. Avoid it when data has a long tail on one side, because outliers hide themselves. Example, Airbnb price, with mean one fifty two seventy two and standard deviation two forty fifteen. A price of ten thousand dollars has a z of forty one, so it is an outlier. A price of five hundred has a z of one point four five, so it is not. The limit is mean plus three standard deviations, eight seventy three dollars. A safer version uses the median instead of the mean, the modified Z, flagged if above three point five. In short, Z score only catches prices above eight seventy three, and a five hundred dollar home looks normal to it.
11: The I Q R rule, which uses box plot fences. For price, Q one is sixty nine dollars and Q three is one seventy five. The I Q R is Q three minus Q one, one hundred six. The lower fence is Q one minus one point five times I Q R, which is minus ninety dollars, and the upper fence is Q three plus one point five times I Q R, three thirty four dollars. Outside the fences means outlier. Big values do not move Q one and Q three, so this rule is not fooled. A five hundred dollar price is above three thirty four, an outlier, and so is ten thousand. There are no low outliers, because the lower fence is below zero dollars. The I Q R flags two thousand nine hundred seventy two listings, almost eight times more than Z score.
12: Z score versus I Q R on all six features. Outliers flagged per feature: for price, Z score finds three eighty eight and I Q R finds two thousand nine hundred seventy two. For minimum nights, three twenty seven versus six thousand six hundred seven. For number of reviews, twelve twenty one versus six thousand twenty one. For host listings, six eighty versus seven thousand eighty one. For availability, zero for both. The skewness values are high for almost every column, nineteen for price, nearly twenty two for minimum nights, so all columns have a long right tail, and we should use I Q R here. In short, on long tailed data, the Z score always finds fewer outliers than I Q R.
13: Why does the Z score miss outliers? This is called masking. Three ten thousand dollar homes make the standard deviation big, two forty dollars. A big standard deviation pushes the Z limit up to eight seventy three dollars. The outliers stretch the ruler that measures them, so they hide. Q one and Q three do not stretch, so I Q R is not fooled. The simple rule: Z score for bell shaped data, I Q R for long tailed data. In short, two thousand five hundred eighty four homes priced between three thirty four and eight seventy three dollars are outliers by I Q R, but the Z score cannot see them.
14: Find outliers with machine learning: three models, shown on three thousand random Airbnb homes using two columns, with red rings around the outliers found. Isolation Forest keeps cutting the data at random, and odd points get separated very quickly. You set the percentage of outliers expected. Local Outlier Factor says a point that is far more alone than its neighbours is an outlier. You set the number of neighbours. D B SCAN makes groups, or clusters, and points that fit no group are outliers. You set the group distance and size.
15: Simple rules versus machine learning models. Z score looks at one column, you choose the limit three, it is good for bell shaped data, and it misses outliers in long tailed data. I Q R looks at one column, you choose the fence size, it is good for long tailed data, but gives no low outliers if the fence is below zero. Isolation Forest looks at many columns, you choose the percentage of outliers, it is good at odd combinations and is fast, but always flags the percentage you set. L O F looks at many columns, you choose the number of neighbours, it is good for points odd for their neighbourhood, and needs scaled data. D B SCAN looks at many columns, you choose eps and min samples, it finds points outside groups, and the result changes with eps. All three models give minus one for an outlier and one for a normal point. In short, one column, use a rule. An odd mix of many columns, use a model.
16: What if we do not fix outliers? Six problems. One, a wrong average: the mean price is one fifty three versus a median of one oh six, so the average looks forty four percent too high. Two, spread looks too big: the standard deviation is two forty dollars before and only eighty four after fixing, almost three times too big. Three, very lopsided data: a skew of nineteen makes tests that expect a bell curve give wrong answers. Four, the regression line gets pulled: just one bad row can flip the line. Five, distance based methods fail: K N N, K means and scaling are controlled by a few huge values. Six, error scores mislead: M S E and R M S E square the errors, so a few rows decide the score. If we ignore outliers, we get wrong numbers, wrong charts and wrong models.
17: Ways to fix outliers. Remove: delete the row, when it is a clear mistake and only a few rows. Cap with I Q R: bring the value down to the fence, to keep every row but shrink big values. Winsorize: cap at the top one percent and bottom one percent, for lighter capping. Median: replace with the middle value, when the value is wrong and the true value is unknown. Group median: replace with its group's middle value, when groups differ, such as room type. K N N: use the average of five similar rows, when similar rows exist. Regression: predict it from other columns, when other columns predict it well. Log: squeeze big values with log of one plus x, when values are real but very spread. Flag: add a zero one column called is outlier, when the outlier itself is useful information. Only removal loses rows. Capping and replacing keep all the data.
18: Which fix? First ask why. Is it a mistake? For example, price zero or minimum nights twelve fifty. Correct it if you can. If not, remove it or replace it with the median. Is it real? For example, a ten thousand dollar luxury penthouse. Keep it, but cap it or use log so it does not control the model. Is it a limit? For example, a house value stored as five hundred thousand and one. Mark it with an is capped column, or drop it, because we do not know the true value. Do not delete a value just because a rule flagged it. Check why first.

31: Lab step eleven: model accuracy before versus after. The same linear model, the same data split, and only the outlier fix changes. Higher R squared is better and lower M A E is better. Raw data: R squared point one two, M A E seventy one dollars. I Q R capped: point four four, forty six dollars. Winsorized: point three. Median imputed: point four one, thirty eight dollars. Group median: point four seven, thirty six dollars. K N N imputed: point four nine, thirty seven dollars. Regression imputed: point four eight, thirty five dollars. Fixing outliers made the model about four times better, R squared from point one two to point four nine, and it halved the error.
32: Key takeaways. One, an outlier is far from the rest, unusual but not always wrong. Two, causes are typing mistakes, rare real values, limits, or a different group. Three, types are global, contextual, collective and multivariate. Four, the Z score works for bell shaped data but misses outliers in long tailed data. Five, I Q R is safer, because big values do not move its fences. Six, ignoring outliers gives a wrong mean and standard deviation, even a flipped regression line. Seven, fix by cause: mistakes get fixed or removed, real values get capped or logged, and limits get flagged. Eight, always compare before versus after: skew nineteen to one, R squared point one two to point four four. Nine, machine learning models look at many columns together and find cases simple rules miss. And ten, K N N and regression give each outlier a smart new value, but check it makes sense.
